title: Cold Soybean Noodle Soup
summary: White soybeans soaked, boiled and blended. Boil them too long and they turn beany.
intro:
Kong-guksu stands or falls on how long the beans boil. Under-boiled they taste beany; over-boiled they smell of meju, the dried fermented soybean block.

Soaked beans go into boiling water for 8 minutes. The moment one crushes under your finger, lift them out. Anything past that is a loss.
steps: Rinse the soybeans and soak them in cold water: 6 hours in summer, 8 hours in winter. They are ready when they have swollen to twice their size.
Rub the soaked beans between your hands to slip the skins off. Pour off the skins as they float to the surface. Skinned beans give a much nuttier, finer broth.
Bring a generous amount of water to a boil, add the beans and boil for 8 minutes. Leave the lid off — it boils over easily.
Fish out one bean and press it with your finger. If it crushes with no resistance, drain them in a sieve straight away.
Rinse under cold water and cool them completely. Blending them while hot brings out a beany smell.
Blend the beans with 700 mL (3 cups) water, the peanuts and the salt for at least 2 minutes, until smooth. Rubbed between your fingertips it should feel free of any grit.
If the texture still bothers you, pass it once through a fine sieve. Chill it in the fridge for at least an hour.
Boil the somyeon, rinse and rub the noodles under cold water, and drain them well.
Put the noodles in a bowl and pour the cold soy broth over. Top with julienned cucumber and sesame seeds.
tips: Rather than salting the broth in advance, it is better for each person to salt their own at the table. Once salted, soy broth tastes saltier as it stands.
Floating ice in it waters the broth down. Chill the soy broth thoroughly ahead of time instead.
Leftover soy broth keeps for up to 2 days in the fridge. If it separates, shake it and use it.
